analysis.one_liner: Treats companies that reincorporate abroad on paper as US companies for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 2019-2021 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a US company buys a foreign company and moves its legal headquarters overseas—usually to a country with much lower taxes—it stops paying US corporate tax on most of its income. This bill would rewrite the rules so that any company doing this after May 2014, where former US owners keep more than half the stock or top management stays in the US, is still treated as a US company for tax purposes. That means inverted companies would keep paying US taxes on their income. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2019 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the bill passes, because companies that keep their operations and management in the United States would continue paying the corporate taxes that fund public services, instead of shifting their tax bill onto everyone else. US companies that stay and pay their taxes also benefit from a more level playing field against rivals that relocate on paper to avoid taxes.

how_it_helps.text: Treats a foreign corporation as a US corporation for tax purposes if former US shareholders hold more than 50% of its stock after the deal, or if the group's management and control remain primarily in the US with significant domestic business activities [S2] [S3].
Applies to inversions completed after May 8, 2014, and to taxable years ending after that date, closing off reincorporations that have already happened [S2] [S3].
Keeps a narrow exception for companies with substantial business activities in the country where they reincorporated, so firms with real foreign operations are not swept in [S3].

Gives the Treasury Department authority to write regulations defining 'management and control' in the US, including a rule that management counts as US-based when top executives making day-to-day strategic decisions are located in the US regardless of title [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US companies that have moved or would move their legal headquarters abroad to lower their tax bills—concentrated in industries like pharmaceuticals, technology, and consumer products—would pay higher US taxes on their worldwide income. Their shareholders bear the cost, and tax-avoidance law and accounting firms would lose a line of business.

drawbacks.text: The bill treats transactions already completed after May 8, 2014 as inverted retroactively, applying to taxable years ending after that date, which raises the concern that companies that structured deals under existing law would face a new tax bill for past years [S3].

Critics of anti-inversion rules argue that US-based taxation of companies with real foreign operations makes them less competitive against foreign rivals in international markets, and that Congress should instead fix the underlying US corporate tax rate that drives companies abroad in the first place.

The bill would raise substantial revenue only from a subset of inverted firms; companies can still use many other legal techniques to shift profits offshore, so by itself it does not solve the broader problem of corporate profit-shifting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: companies that keep their real operations and management in the US would no longer escape US taxes by relocating on paper, and the revenue supports public services everyone uses. The main legitimate costs are the retroactive application to deals struck after May 2014 and the possibility that some firms with genuinely mixed operations get drawn in, though the bill's substantial-business-activities exception limits that. On balance the bill is a targeted fix to a specific avoidance technique, not a comprehensive overhaul of corporate taxation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2019, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Stop Corporate Inversions Act of 2019 on July 17, 2019, with 11 Democratic cosponsors and one Independent cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action—not a hearing, not a committee vote, not a floor vote—was ever recorded, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

The bill would have treated foreign corporations formed by inversions after May 8, 2014 as US corporations for tax purposes if former US owners kept majority ownership or if management and significant business activity remained in the US [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that have reincorporated abroad to lower their US tax bills—and their shareholders—remain better off, since the tax rules this bill would have changed stayed untouched and no corporate tax revenue was collected under it.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican sponsored it, and the Republican-run Finance Committee and Senate majority never acted on it.

industries.industry: Inverted corporations (US companies that reincorporated abroad, e.g. in pharmaceuticals and medical devices)
industries.note: The bill would tax them as US corporations, raising their tax bill on worldwide income. Their savings from tax-dodging reincorporation come at the expense of the general taxpayer base.

industries.industry: Corporate tax planning advisers (law and accounting firms specializing in cross-border structuring)
industries.note: Anti-inversion rules would shrink the market for restructuring deals designed to relocate a company's legal domicile to a low-tax country.

industries.industry: US multinational competitors that stayed domiciled in the US
industries.note: Leveling the field so rivals cannot escape US tax by reincorporating abroad removes a competitive disadvantage for companies that pay their US taxes.
